title: How to Die Having Never Lived
html:
“‘I have led a toothless life’, he thought. ‘A toothless life. I have never bitten into anything. I was waiting. I was reserving myself for later on—and I have just noticed that my teeth have gone.’” — Jean-Paul Sartre, The Age of Reason

Life is a navigation problem—a perpetual battle of what to do and where to go.

We can approach this problem in one of (roughly) two ways: we can either increase the probability of good things happening—willfully absorbing the blows synonymous with personal development and the unknown—or we can decrease the probability of experiencing pain—half-participating, glancing off life’s many surfaces without daring to experience any of them fully. While no approach is wrong in the moral sense of the word, only one yields a life well-lived.

Avoiding pain can keep us alive, so, to that end, it makes sense. But the fear and anxiety that kept our ancestors out of the tiger’s jaws can rob us of the gumption to pursue the best that life has to offer. What satisfaction is there in perennial dabbling—a little of this; a little of that—without ever tasting mastery? Are we content to keep everyone at arm’s length, never letting them grant us the privilege of being seen? If we commit ourselves to a life of half-asleep dithering, we never commit ourselves to anything at all. And it is this decision—or, indecision, rather—rooted in a feeble avoidance of pain, that lets life pass us by, without us ever having bitten into anything.

In contrast, increasing our surface area for good things to happen requires courage and commitment. Commitment—unfettered engagement—precedes all of life’s meaningful assets: relationships, health, knowledge, wealth, reputation, etc. None can exist without it. We need courage to complement commitment because we know whichever path we walk will be laden with snakes, and that, no matter the path we choose, it will be hard, and it will hurt. There are no free lunches. Every relationship fractures, and every ounce of expertise gained in one domain costs ignorance elsewhere. Still, we must schlep onwards, taking stock of our open doors—the affordances of who we are in this moment—and commit, walking through one door and shutting all others. Our ability to progress through life depends on our courage to choose. And choices beget choices, so we must choose again… and again… and again to let better, more actualized versions of ourselves become real.

So why then, if our best lives hide behind curtains of commitment, does the thought of it paralyze us? Because when we commit, we kill our selves. Not our actual selves, but potential ones. And then we are forced to grieve the loss of everyone we could have been but will no longer get the chance to be. To decide, decidere in Latin, means to cut off, and with each decision—each cut—versions of ourselves that we may have one day been bleed out and die. It is a heavy burden to look into the hopeful eyes of distant versions of ourselves—whose fists drum on the glass between imagination and reality—and tell them, “No. You don’t get to exist.” Saying no hurts, but it hurts more never to say yes—to keep all our potential selves trapped behind the glass until, one by one, they disappear, and the drumming recedes from a monstrous roar to a mousey patter. And then all becomes quiet, and we are out of time. We missed our chances. Our teeth have gone.

To die having never lived, we need only wait. We need only play games of continual avoidance—masquerading as exploration—that shield us from the grief of committing. But I would wager that, if you are reading this, this is not the kind of life you want to live. So play time is over.

Let go.

Jump in.

Know that decisions are not shackles.

We can commit to something knowing it may not serve us forever. And we can renew our commitment each day while it still does. But if the day arrives when a commitment no longer serves us, we can detach with gratitude, enriched by the depths of what it bore. And we will be better for it; no wasted opportunities, no wasted life.

It is better to become someone, and then someone else, than to never become anybody at all.

“Give your heart then change your mind/you’re allowed to do it/cause God knows it’s been done to you, and somehow you got through it.” — John Mayer, The Age of Worry
